lessons.title: Latin: girls and water
lessons.body:
## The first declension

Most first-declension nouns end in *-a* and are feminine: *puella* (girl), *aqua* (water), *via* (road). The ablative singular has a long vowel: *puellā*. In this course macrons are always printed, but you never have to type them: an answer without them is marked right, with a note showing the full spelling.

> *Puella aquam portat.* — The girl carries water.

## Saying it

The course teaches two pronunciations. Pick yours with the **Pronunciation** switch at the top of the lesson; the paragraphs below change with it.

```pron restored
**Restored classical.** *c* is always hard, as in English *cat*: *Cicerō* is [ˈkɪkɛroː]. *v* is English *w*: *vīnum* [ˈwiːnʊm]. *ae* rhymes with English *eye*: *puellae* [pʊˈɛllaɪ̯].
```

```pron ecclesiastical
**Ecclesiastical (church Latin).** *c* before *e* or *i* is English *ch*: *Cicerō* is [ˈtʃitʃero]. *v* is English *v*: *vīnum* [ˈvinum]. *ae* sounds like *e* in *bet*: *puellae* [puˈɛlle].
```

The genitive *puellae* ends in {pron=restored}[aɪ̯], like *eye*{/pron}{pron=ecclesiastical}[e], like *bet*{/pron}.

```speak
# Say it
Puella aquam portat.
= The girl carries water.
Amō puellam.
= I love the girl.
```

The recordings you hear are a computer voice reading Latin as if it were Italian, so they're only approximate.

lessons.title: Greek: first words
lessons.body:
## Greek words

Greek is written here in full polytonic spelling: breathings, accents and the iota subscript. Type it in **Beta Code**: letters, then the marks after each letter.

| You type | You get |
|---|---|
| `a)nh/r` | *ἀνήρ* |
| `w)|dh/` | *ᾠδή* |
| `*(ella/s` | *Ἑλλάς* |
| `r(h/twr` | *ῥήτωρ* |
| `tw=| a)nqrw/pw|` | *τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ* |

Final sigma is automatic: `lo/gos` gives *λόγος*. Accents and breathings are optional in answers, so *ανθρωπου* is marked right, with a note giving *ἀνθρώπου*.

> *ὁ ἄνθρωπος λέγει.* — The man speaks.

A word in Latin letters, such as the transliteration *anthrōpos*, is marked as a transliteration for screen readers.

questions.explanation: puellā, with a long final ā.
ἀνθρώπου: the accent moves to the penult because the ending is long.
